claims.text: Thermogravimetric analysis can be used to assess high-temperature oxidation behavior.
High-temperature X-ray diffraction can be used to assess phase stability.
TGA continuously monitors weight changes caused by oxidation.
HT-XRD can detect phase evolution during high-temperature exposure.
Temperatures above approximately 800°C are high enough to initiate oxidation in the unspecified material.
High-temperature exposure in an oxidizing atmosphere forms oxide scales.
High-temperature exposure produces phase transformations within the material.
Oxidation results in a mass gain detectable by TGA.
Oxidation induces structural changes that can be tracked by HT-XRD.
Combining TGA and HT-XRD allows weight changes to be correlated with phase evolution.
Oxide formation will produce a measurable weight gain.
High-temperature oxidation will be accompanied by detectable phase transitions in the diffraction patterns.
Testing under an inert atmosphere should produce negligible mass change.
Testing under an inert atmosphere should produce negligible phase alteration.
The approach is applicable only when oxidation kinetics fall within the detection limits of TGA.
Rapid sublimation or evaporation of material components can interfere with TGA or XRD signals.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis presents HT-XRD as a method for assessing phase stability, but the predicted outcome requires detectable phase transitions and the falsification rule treats failure to detect phase changes as failure of the method. A genuinely phase-stable material could show no transition while still being successfully assessed by HT-XRD.
